rule.title: Centralized AppError Exception Hierarchy
rule.statement: Application errors must instantiate or subclass AppError, encapsulating HTTP statusCode, a machine-readable errorCode, and a safe client message.
rule.rationale: Throwing raw Error instances or string literals causes unhandled promise rejections, inconsistent error responses, and potential server crashes.
rule.implementation_guidance: Throw new AppError(404, 'DOCUMENT_NOT_FOUND', 'Document does not exist'). Let Global Error Middleware catch and format it.

forbidden.example: throw new Error('something went wrong'); // Missing HTTP status and machine error code

preferred.example: throw new AppError(404, 'NOT_FOUND', 'Knowledge Base not found');

source.book_title: Design and Build Great Web APIs
source.evidence_quote: Errors should be treated as first-class citizens. Creating structured error representations with HTTP status codes makes debugging predictable.

rule.title: Never Expose Internal Stack Traces in Production
rule.statement: Production error responses must never expose raw stack traces, SQL queries, database column names, or internal file system paths.
rule.rationale: Stack traces expose internal architecture, database schema, and third-party library versions to potential attackers, facilitating exploit discovery.
rule.implementation_guidance: In production (NODE_ENV === 'production'), log the full stack trace to Winston and return a generic 500 error payload.

forbidden.example: { error: err.stack, sql: 'SELECT * FROM users WHERE...' }

preferred.example: { success: false, error: { code: 'INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR', message: 'An unexpected error occurred.' } }

source.chapter: Chapter 7: Error Handling and Information Leakage
source.evidence_quote: Stack traces and internal system details must never be returned to the client in production. They provide adversaries with valuable reconnaissance information.
